claims.text: The starting alloy has the atomic composition W38Ta36Cr15V11.
The starting alloy has a single-phase BCC structure.
The starting alloy is nanocrystalline and has high grain-boundary density.
The starting alloy can be produced by powder processing.
The intervention is to add 0.5 vol% Y2O3 nanoparticles by in-situ powder mixing before spark plasma sintering.
The processing route will produce a uniform Y2O3 dispersion at grain boundaries and within grains.
Irradiation produces vacancies, interstitials, and defect clusters, while boundaries and other sinks can absorb point defects.
Y2O3 nanoparticles in W38Ta36Cr15V11 will act as sinks for irradiation-induced vacancies and interstitials.
Defect absorption by Y2O3 will reduce the supersaturation driving Cr and V segregation and precipitation.
Y2O3 nanoparticles will pin grain boundaries and control microstructural evolution.
Grain-boundary pinning by Y2O3 will aid densification and improve bulk fabricability.
Unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11 develops a Cr- and V-rich second phase and Cr/V segregation at grain boundaries and triple junctions under irradiation up to 8 dpa.
The unmodified alloy shows no irradiation-induced dislocation loops under the reported irradiation conditions.
The unmodified alloy exhibits negligible irradiation hardening.
At approximately 8 dpa, Y2O3 addition will reduce precipitate volume fraction by more than 50% relative to the unmodified alloy.
The modified alloy will retain minimal irradiation-induced defect density and negligible irradiation hardening.
The proposed effect applies after spark plasma sintering at about 1500°C and 100 MPa followed by 1 MeV irradiation at 400–600°C to about 8 dpa.
The effectiveness may vary significantly outside the specified processing temperature, pressure, irradiation-temperature, and dose window.
